1.pericope_label: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars; Whilst their children remember their altars and their groves by the green trees upon the high hills. O my mountain in the field, I will give thy substance and all thy treasures to the spoil, and thy high places for sin, throughout all thy borders. And thou, even thyself, shalt discontinue from thine heritage that I gave thee; and I will cause thee to serve thine enemies in the land which thou knowest not: for ye have kindled a fire in mine anger, which shall burn for ever.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the sin as the sinful practice rather than a proneness to it, derive the graving word from a root meaning to scratch, and distribute the clauses so that the table of the heart belongs with the pen of iron and the horns of the altars with the diamond point; Ellicott identifies the tools, adjudicates the clause about the children in favour of the children doing the remembering, makes the mountain a poetic name for Zion whose greatness is in being the mountain of Jehovah, and completes the irony of the sabbath rest of the land.

Gill reports the rendering that makes the children a comparison rather than the subject and presses it to the point that they loved their idols better than their offspring, and allows the mountain to be either the temple or the city; Calvin makes the engraving a measure of degree, since a light besprinkling of vice leaves a remedy while iniquity cut into the marrow leaves none, refuses the vocative reading of the mountain, and makes the loss worse than death.

Clarke identifies the sin as idolatry and takes the mountainous land, though the city may be meant; Wesley explains the horns of the altar twice over, from the blood of sacrifices sprinkled on them or from an inscription naming the idol.

Henry sets the passage as a courtroom answer to their own question what their iniquity was, the indictment now proved, too plain to be denied and too bad to be excused, on record in God's omniscience and in their own conscience alike.

debates.question: Who does the remembering in the clause about the children?

positions.position: It is a comparison: as they remember their children, so they remember their altars, and they loved the idols better.
The children remember, which is more natural and better supported by the versions.
The children remember, the iniquity running down to posterity by a kind of hereditary right.

debates.question: What is the mountain in the field?

positions.position: Either the temple, called the mountain of the house, or the city on a hill in the midst of a plain.
The mountainous land, though the city itself may be meant.
A poetic name for Zion, whose greatness lies in being the mountain of Jehovah.
Not a vocative at all: the sense is that the mountains shall be as the fields, and no hiding-place will serve.

debates.question: What does the word for discontinuing carry?

positions.position: The law of the seventh year: because Judah broke it, the Lord will make them loose their hold of the inheritance.
The same practices, with the irony that the land will now enjoy the sabbaths the people withheld.
A loss worse than death, some remaining alive to be scattered, perishing living and seeing.

outliers.claim: Distributes the two clauses between the two instruments: the table of the heart belongs with the pen of iron, the horns of the altars with the diamond point.

Gives two reasons why the sin should be said to be engraven on the horns of the altar: the blood of sacrifices offered to idols was sprinkled there, or the altars carried an inscription naming the idol.

themes: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars;
Whilst their children remember their altars and their groves by the green trees upon the high hills.
O my mountain in the field, I will give thy substance and all thy treasures to the spoil, and thy high places for sin, throughout all thy borders.

And thou, even thyself, shalt discontinue from thine heritage that I gave thee; and I will cause thee to serve thine enemies in the land which thou knowest not: for ye have kindled a fire in mine anger, which shall burn for ever.

5.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord. For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch map the section, the sources of ruin and of well-being to the eighteenth verse and the way to life thereafter; Ellicott calls the curse vehement and abrupt, a naming of the root evil that produced the foreign alliances, notes that two different words stand behind the English man, and adjudicates the disputed shrub on literary grounds, since a man being like a destitute man is a weak similitude while the bare shrub balances the tree planted by the waters.

Gill runs the versions on the shrub and settles for ling or heath, a low plant of waste ground reckoned by the naturalist among the unhappy plants forbidden for sacred use; Calvin hears the second word for man as contemptuous, thinks the prophet prefixed this sentence to many discourses because promises and threatenings alike were disregarded, and concludes only that the shrub was useless and now unknown, rejecting the juniper because fruit grows on its branches.

Clarke narrows the reference to the Egyptian alliance and then widens it to whoever trusts an arm of flesh for the salvation of his soul, and abandons the shrub for a blasted tree, adding a physiology by which the drought has left it unable to absorb more juices.

Henry treats the passage as a practical sermon of which we have only the heads, defines the sin as giving to men the confidence that belongs to God's attributes alone, presses every sense of the word flesh, and finds the malignity in an evil heart of unbelief that calls God its hope with the mouth while the heart withdraws.

debates.question: What is the plant the cursed man is likened to?

positions.position: Ling or heath, a low shrub of waste ground, fruitless and seedless.
Not a shrub but a blasted tree, parched and withered.
A useless shrub now unknown, certainly not the juniper, since fruit grows on its branches.
Either a destitute man or a bare shrub; the shrub is the bolder similitude and balances the tree, and there is something weak in saying a man shall be like a destitute man.

debates.question: Why does this sentence stand here?

positions.position: Because the prophet prefixed it to many discourses, writing once for all what he had often said to a people who disregarded promise and threat alike.
Because the section is planned, running to the eighteenth verse on the sources of ruin and well-being and thence to the end on the way to life.
Because it names the root evil that had eaten into the people's life and produced the foreign alliances.

outliers.claim: Presses every sense of the word flesh: weak as flesh without bone or sinew, inactive as flesh without spirit, mortal as flesh that soon corrupts, and false besides.
Notes that two different words stand behind the English man in this verse, the first implying strength and the second weakness.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord.
For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.

7.pericope_label: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the Lord, and whose hope the Lord is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the Lord search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch call the portrait of the blessed man an extension of the psalm's picture, and defend the conjunction before the clause about requital, absent from many manuscripts and from the old translators, on the ground that it sets the aim apart with the prominence of an independent thought; Ellicott hears the psalm behind the beatitude and names the arrangement the prophet's own Ebal and Gerizim, renders the heart incurably diseased rather than desperately wicked, and would drop that same conjunction so that the closing words explain what went before.

Gill turns the tree christological, planted not by ministers who plant and water instrumentally but by the Lord as efficient cause, describes the heart's fraud in proposing sin under the notion of pleasure, and argues that since Christ searches the reins he must be Jehovah; Calvin notices the pedagogical order, that the false confidence had to be pulled up before this could be sown, and warns against the common habit of mutilating the verse about the heart without regard to the prophet's design.

Clarke explains how roots spread by the river keep a tree green through any drought, holds the received rendering of the heart simply wrong since the Hebrew never denotes wickedness but rather what is wretched or feeble, and notes that the apostles called God the Knower of the heart; Wesley keeps the strong word and adds the double unsearchableness, that a man knows neither his own heart nor his neighbour's.

debates.question: How should the second word describing the heart be rendered?

positions.position: Not as wickedness at all: the Hebrew never denotes it, and the sense is wretched or feeble, distressed beyond all things.
Incurably diseased, wickedness being implied as a taint following the deliberate choice rather than the choice itself.
Abominably wicked, and unsearchable both to oneself and to one's neighbour.

debates.question: Should the conjunction before the clause about requital stand?

positions.position: It should be dropped, so that the closing words explain the singular way that precedes them.
It should stand, since it sets the aim apart and gives it the prominence of an independent thought.

debates.question: Why is the heart brought in here?

positions.position: Because it answers why a man chooses the curse rather than the blessing, self-deceit blinding his perception of good and evil.
Because it is the source of the idolatry and creature-confidence already charged.
Because the prophet had a particular necessity in view, which must be understood before any general doctrine is drawn from the words.

outliers.claim: Names the arrangement the prophet's own Ebal and Gerizim, and draws out the chiasm: as the blasted heath sees no good, so the tree sees no evil.

Notices the order of teaching, that the second part could not have been taught profitably until the false confidence was pulled up, since seed cast on uncultivated soil bears nothing and the plough must go before the seed.

themes: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the Lord, and whose hope the Lord is.

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
I the Lord search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.

11.pericope_label: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool. A glorious high throne from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary. O Lord, the hope of Israel, all that forsake thee shall be ashamed, and they that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch prefer the apostrophe in the verse about the throne because it suits the tension of feeling in the discourse, allowing that the older reading as a plain statement is grammatically defensible, and fix the place of the sanctuary as the temple and not heaven; Ellicott renders the bird as heaping up eggs she has not laid, reports the popular belief behind it and admits that modern naturalists have not observed the habit, joins the throne verse to the next as a string of vocatives, and recovers the eastern practice of writing on the ground.

Gill takes the other construction of the bird, eggs sat on and never hatched, and passes on a Jewish reading that supplies a particle of comparison so that the temple is like a glorious high throne with heaven as the throne itself; Calvin makes the last word a thing of nought, so that the covetous man becomes a mockery, and ties the praise of the nation to the charge against it, since the more bountifully God dealt with them the more atrocious was the ingratitude.

Clarke reports two translators who make the bird hatch what it did not lay and draws the moral that the young desert a bird which is not their mother, keeps the fool and adds that he shall be reputed such, having lost his soul for wealth he never enjoyed, and reads the writing in the earth as names in dust that the first wind will efface; Wesley takes the eggs as lost by man or beast, makes the folly retrospective, and reads the writing as portion rather than record, such having nothing beyond the earth.

Henry explains the shape of the passage rather than its parts: the prophet is retired for private meditation, as ministers who would have comfort in their work must often be, and takes the liberty devout souls use in soliloquy, passing from one thing to another without tying himself strictly to the laws of method and coherence.

positions.position: Heaps up eggs she has not laid, on a popular belief that the partridge steals other birds' eggs and is deserted by the broods.
Hatches what it did not lay, so that the young desert a bird which is not their mother.
Sits on eggs and never hatches them, having lost them by accident or to man or beast.

debates.question: How do the words about the throne stand?

positions.position: As a string of vocatives joined to the next verse, the supplied verb being dropped.
As an apostrophe, which suits the tension of feeling, though the older reading as a statement is grammatically defensible.
With a particle of comparison supplied, so that the temple is like a glorious high throne and heaven is the throne itself.

debates.question: What is it to be written in the earth?

positions.position: Erasure: names written in dust that the first wind will mar past reading.
A contrast with a name graven on rock, drawn from the eastern habit of writing on the ground.
Portion rather than record: such shall have nothing beyond the earth.

outliers.claim: Admits that modern naturalists have not observed the habit ascribed to the partridge, and suggests the belief arose from the cuckoo laying its eggs in her nest.
Explains why Scripture rehearses blessings at all, with a twofold object: to persuade us that he who begins the work will finish it, and to move us to render thanks.

themes: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.
A glorious high throne from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary.
O Lord, the hope of Israel, all that forsake thee shall be ashamed, and they that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living waters.

14.pericope_label: Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise. Behold, they say unto me, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now. As for me, I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee: neither have I desired the woeful day; thou knowest: that which came out of my lips was right before thee. Be not a terror unto me: thou art my hope in the day of evil. Let them be confounded that persecute me, but let not me be confounded: let them be dismayed, but let not me be dismayed: bring upon them the day of evil, and destroy them with double destruction.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch ground the whole prayer on one thing, that the Lord should not shame his prophet by leaving the prophecies against Judah unfulfilled, God being his refuge in the day of evil; Ellicott makes the healing a contrast with the deserters, infers a date from the mockers' taunt, calls the English of the shepherd clause obscure and offers both a figurative and a literal rendering, and reads the terror as the prospect of an unfulfilled message and a by-word messenger.

Gill takes the healing of the prophet's own sins and of the wound his people's sins had made in him, and reads the shepherd clause as his not having been importunate to be dismissed from a thankless service; Calvin makes the prayer self-preservation in a country where every turn offered what would allure him away, diagnoses the misuse of God's forbearance among the reprobate, and justifies the imprecation by the public character of the quarrel.

Clarke answers the mockers from history, that the events did take place and every tittle of the menace was fulfilled, follows a translator who makes the shepherd clause a refusal to outrun God's guidance, reads the petition about terror as a plea against the commission itself, and defuses the closing curse as prediction rather than prayer; Wesley keeps the last clause of the prayer for praise and balances the shepherd clause, that he neither sought the office nor declined it.

debates.question: What is the prophet asking to be healed of?

positions.position: His own sins and his share in a corrupt time, or the wound his people's sins had made in him.
The same need as the deserters have, but sought where it can be found.
The danger of being carried away, apostasy prevailing on every side.

debates.question: What does the clause about the shepherd mean?

positions.position: That he had not been importunate to be dismissed from the service.
That he had not been in haste to outrun God's guidance, nor wished the calamity to come quickly.
That he neither sought the office nor declined it when called.
That he had not been quick to withdraw from the work; or, on a bolder reading, that the shepherding was literal and he had been employed in the pasture grounds of his priestly town.

debates.question: What is the terror he asks God not to be?

positions.position: Desertion, God withdrawing his presence or leaving the message unfulfilled and the messenger a by-word.
The commission itself: do not command me to predict miseries and then abandon me to them and to my enemies.

outliers.claim: Defuses the closing imprecation by grammar: the words are to be understood as simple predictions rather than prayers, so that they shall be confounded rather than let them be.

Explains why the prayer against the persecutors is not private: crying out against the avaricious raised all who lived by plunder, speaking against lust raised a second conspiracy, and condemning drunkenness a third.

themes: Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise.
Behold, they say unto me, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now.
As for me, I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee: neither have I desired the woeful day; thou knowest: that which came out of my lips was right before thee.
Be not a terror unto me: thou art my hope in the day of evil.
Let them be confounded that persecute me, but let not me be confounded: let them be dismayed, but let not me be dismayed: bring upon them the day of evil, and destroy them with double destruction.

19.pericope_label: Thus said the Lord unto me; Go and stand in the gate of the children of the people, whereby the kings of Judah come in, and by the which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem; And say unto them, Hear ye the word of the Lord, ye kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that enter in by these gates: Thus saith the Lord; Take heed to yourselves, and bear no burden on the sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem; Neither carry forth a burden out of your houses on the sabbath day, neither do ye any work, but hallow ye the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers. But they obeyed not, neither inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff, that they might not hear, nor receive instruction.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes this the opening of a fresh series arranged in chronological order, dates it from the promises to the early years of the reign that followed the reformation, points out that no gate so described appears in the topographical record, and fills in the sabbath traffic from a later parallel, the day kept after a fashion but turned into a market.

Gill calls it a fresh sermon and a very proper place to have begun a new chapter, refuses to restrict the burden to dirt and soil, and reads the charge as addressed to the inward frame of the soul; Calvin complains that whoever divided the chapters was deficient in judgment here as elsewhere, raises and answers the objection that resting one day is a small matter, and turns the appeal to the fathers round, since children are less excusable for following bad examples.

Clarke takes the gate for the most public one, notes that eight manuscripts and two versions omit the clause naming all Judah beside the kings, and makes the breach of the sabbath the cause of the whole ruin, since it led to neglect of sacrifice and of all public worship and so let in the flood of wrath.

Henry dates the message to the reforming reign, since such promises are scarcely found when matters come nearer the extremity, and explains why gates are chosen: the courts were kept and the stores laid up there, and the proclamation begins, as a king's does, at the court gate.

debates.question: When was this sabbath sermon delivered?

positions.position: Under the reforming king, for the furtherance of that work, since such promises are scarcely found nearer the extremity.
In the early years of the reign that followed, before the sins had taken the hopeless character of the previous chapters.

debates.question: Why is so much made of an outward rite?

positions.position: Because these men were not hypocrites about it but violated the day openly, having grown so lost as to pretend no religion at all.
Because the breach led to neglect of sacrifice and of all public worship, and so brought all immorality with it.
Because the charge is addressed to the inward frame of the soul, which must be disposed for the work of the day.

outliers.claim: Complains that whoever divided the chapters was deficient in judgment here as in many other places, this discourse being plainly separate from what precedes.

Reconstructs the sabbath traffic from a later parallel: baskets of fruit and fish brought in by villagers coming up to the services, and the city's wares carried to the gates to be sold to them, so that the day was turned into a market.

themes: Thus said the Lord unto me; Go and stand in the gate of the children of the people, whereby the kings of Judah come in, and by the which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem;
And say unto them, Hear ye the word of the Lord, ye kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that enter in by these gates:
Thus saith the Lord; Take heed to yourselves, and bear no burden on the sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem;
Neither carry forth a burden out of your houses on the sabbath day, neither do ye any work, but hallow ye the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers.
But they obeyed not, neither inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff, that they might not hear, nor receive instruction.

24.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, if ye diligently hearken unto me, saith the Lord, to bring in no burden through the gates of this city on the sabbath day, but hallow the sabbath day, to do no work therein; Then shall there enter into the gates of this city kings and princes sitting upon the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they, and their princes, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: and this city shall remain for ever. And they shall come from the cities of Judah, and from the places about Jerusalem, and from the land of Benjamin, and from the plain, and from the mountains, and from the south, bringing burnt offerings, and sacrifices, and meat offerings, and incense, and bringing sacrifices of praise, unto the house of the Lord. But if ye will not hearken unto me to hallow the sabbath day, and not to bear a burden, even entering in at the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day; then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem, and it shall not be quenched.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch state the threat plainly, that if the desecration continues the city is to be burnt with fire; Ellicott holds the fire figurative rather than literal, the fierce anger of the Lord that man cannot quench, hears the plural of kings and princes as giving grandeur to a picture of revived majesty, and turns topographer and liturgist on the places and the offerings named.

Gill reads the opening as a concession, that so it shall be notwithstanding all former disobedience; Calvin asks whether resting on the seventh day was of such moment that a kingdom's perpetuity should hang on it and answers that the outward rite carried a spiritual end, takes kingdom and priesthood together as the whole of their happiness, and explains that God first allures and then deals with men according to the hardness of their hearts.

Clarke draws the general rule that though destruction was positively threatened there was an unexpressed proviso throughout, and leaves the responsibility where the sermon leaves it, that their sin lay at their own door.

debates.question: How is the fire in the gates to be taken?

positions.position: Plainly: the city is to be burnt with fire if the desecration continues.
Figuratively rather than literally: the fierce anger of the Lord that man cannot quench, of which a conflagration may have been the instrument.
As the order of God's dealing: he first kindly allures, and then, finding men refractory, deals with them according to the hardness of their hearts.

debates.question: Can so great a promise hang on the sabbath?

positions.position: Only because the outward rite carried a spiritual end, the day being a visible symbol of their sanctification.
The promise is conditional throughout, an unexpressed proviso running under the threatened destruction.
The opening word is itself a concession: so it shall be, notwithstanding all former disobedience.

outliers.claim: Notes that each place named, though descriptive in meaning, was used as definitely as we use the Campagna of Rome or the Weald of Kent, and sorts the offerings into those wholly consumed on the altar and those of which the flesh was eaten.
Takes kingdom and priesthood together as the whole of their happiness, both being types of Christ, since by the one they knew God propitious and by the other that he was the guardian of their safety.

themes: And it shall come to pass, if ye diligently hearken unto me, saith the Lord, to bring in no burden through the gates of this city on the sabbath day, but hallow the sabbath day, to do no work therein;

Then shall there enter into the gates of this city kings and princes sitting upon the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they, and their princes, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: and this city shall remain for ever.

And they shall come from the cities of Judah, and from the places about Jerusalem, and from the land of Benjamin, and from the plain, and from the mountains, and from the south, bringing burnt offerings, and sacrifices, and meat offerings, and incense, and bringing sacrifices of praise, unto the house of the Lord.

But if ye will not hearken unto me to hallow the sabbath day, and not to bear a burden, even entering in at the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day; then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem, and it shall not be quenched.
